summary: Explains why the authentication option is needed for Mobile IPv6 signalling between a mobile node and its home agent, in addition to IPsec protection. It supports the case for the option that secures Binding Update and Binding Acknowledgement messages. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains why a special extra proof-of-identity stamp is worth adding on top of the lock already used in a traveling device's messages.

subtitle: Why cellular networks need simpler authentication for Mobile IPv6.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 originally required IPsec between a mobile device and its home agent, but cellular networks like CDMA2000 and WiMAX found this approach too complex and inefficient.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4285 defines an authentication option that allows Mobile IPv6 to use a simpler authentication mechanism based on shared secrets with an AAA server, similar to Mobile IPv4.
tldr.outcome: This document explains why that simpler approach was needed in certain deployment scenarios, though RFC 4877 later provided IPsec-based alternatives.

today: RFC 5419 remains an informational document explaining the historical context for RFC 4285. It is not itself a standard, but rather a justification for deployment choices made in RFC 4285. The authentication option specified in RFC 4285 is still used in cellular networks, though RFC 4877 provided additional IPsec-based options for environments that prefer them.

sections.title: Why Mobile IPv6 Needs an Authentication Option
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (as defined in RFC 3775) lets a device keep the same IP address while roaming between networks. The protocol originally required IPsec—a strong encryption system—to protect the registration messages between the mobile node and its home agent. However, this requirement posed problems for cellular operators planning to deploy Mobile IPv6 in networks like CDMA2000 and WiMAX.

This document explains why RFC 4285, which defines an authentication option for Mobile IPv6, was specified as an alternative to IPsec-only protection. The authentication option lets home agents authenticate mobile nodes using a simpler mechanism based on a pre-shared secret with an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) backend server.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet devices usually encrypt their password messages strongly. But phone networks already have a simpler, trusted way to check who you are through their own security server. This memo explains why using that simpler way worked well for phones.

sections.title: Motivation for the Authentication Option in Cellular Networks
sections.content:
Cellular operators deploying Mobile IPv6 faced several practical constraints. First, IPsec adds extra data to every message, consuming precious bandwidth on limited air interfaces. Second, establishing an IPsec connection requires multiple message exchanges using IKE (Internet Key Exchange), which adds latency and further strains wireless capacity. Third, many mobile devices already lacked IKE software at the time.

More fundamentally, cellular networks already had working Mobile IPv4 deployments with established AAA infrastructure for authenticating users. Operators wanted Mobile IPv6 to use the same authentication backend and operational model rather than requiring new IPsec management. They also needed the ability to dynamically assign home agents and addresses based on AAA data, which the original Mobile IPv6 specification did not support.

The 3GPP2 (which defines CDMA2000 standards) and WiMAX specifications therefore adopted the authentication option as their preferred security model, alongside Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping mechanisms (RFC 5026) that allow home agents to be assigned dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone networks already use a network-wide directory to check if you should get service. Using that same system for IPv6 was simpler than installing new security software on every device.

sections.title: How CDMA2000 Networks Deploy Mobile IPv6
sections.content:
In a CDMA2000 network, the mobile node is pre-configured with an NAI (Network Access Identifier, like a username) and an MN-AAA key—a secret shared between the device and the home AAA server. When the mobile node sends a Binding Update to register with a home agent, it includes:

  • The NAI identifying the user
  • A timestamp option proving freshness
  • An authenticator computed using HMAC-SHA1 over the message with the MN-AAA key

The home agent forwards the NAI and authenticator to the AAA server, which verifies the user and derives a session key. That key is returned to the home agent, which uses it to authenticate subsequent Binding Acknowledgements and future Binding Updates. This design mirrors Mobile IPv4 authentication, making it familiar to operators already running MIPv4 networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone sends a message signed with a secret only it and the home AAA server know. The server checks that it is really you, creates a temporary key, and sends it to the home agent so they can keep talking securely.

sections.title: Limitations of the Authentication Option
sections.content:
The authentication option has important limitations. It does not support route optimization—the RFC 3775 feature that lets devices communicate directly with other endpoints. Route optimization requires IPsec tunnel mode, so networks using the authentication option must disable it unless link-layer security (like CDMA's own physical-layer encryption) provides equivalent protection.

The authentication option also places security responsibility on the Mobile IPv6 protocol itself rather than delegating it to IPsec, and it relies on timestamps for replay protection, requiring reasonably synchronized clocks. It does not support the wide range of authentication methods that IKEv2 offers, such as certificates or Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP). The mechanism also requires that the MN-AAA shared key and security associations be set up by deployment-specific out-of-band mechanisms not standardized by the IETF, though RFC 3957 addressed similar key derivation for Mobile IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: This simpler method has trade-offs: it does not work well for certain advanced features, it needs clocks to be synchronized, and it depends on how each network sets up its keys.

sections.title: Status and Related Work
sections.content:
This document is informational; it explains the reasoning behind RFC 4285 rather than specifying new protocol mechanisms. When RFC 4285 was being developed, the original Mobile IPv6 specification did not allow dynamic home agent assignment or IKEv2-based IPsec. RFC 4877, published after this justification was written, specified how to use IKEv2 to establish IPsec SAs dynamically and integrated it with AAA backends, addressing some of the original concerns.

However, RFC 4877's approach still carries more overhead than the authentication option, so the authentication option remains useful in bandwidth-constrained or operationally simpler deployments. The same approach is used in WiMAX network architecture. The document notes that some of the motivations are now less pressing with IKEv2 and modern bootstrapping mechanisms available, but argues that the authentication option provides legitimate deployment flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo explains why operators needed a simpler way. Later, better tools came along to make IPsec easier, but the simpler way is still useful when you want to keep things lightweight.
